newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Runaway credit haunts S.African clothing stores.
newsitem.headline: Runaway credit haunts S.African clothing stores.

text.p: Massive growth in credit extension by South African clothing and footwear retailers last year is coming home to roost, eroding company earnings and sending investors scrambling for cover.

The Johannesburg Stock Exchange's stores sector has lost almost 34 percent of its value since the end of January as firms have failed to stir up last year's consumer demand levels won with the introduction of favourable credit terms.
Stubbornly high interest rates, which dimmed the outlook for consumers this year and look to remain high into 1997, have been a further bugbear for retailers.

"The credit extension in previous years was so extensive that now the consumer is under a lot of pressure plus he's had the high interest rates that has made things worse," said Terry Pettit, an analyst at broking firm SBC Warburg.
Analysts said clothing stores had last year extended the payment period on credit to 12 months for the first time, sparking a consumer buying binge.
This had swelled earnings creating a high base off which profits this year had to grow.
"The biggest single factor for companies is this high credit base," said John Biccard, an analyst at Simpson McKie James Capel.
"The earnings figures have been very disappointing, and so companies have been downrated."

South African Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals has on many occasions expressed concern about the country's persistently high levels of credit supply and has warned that interest rates will not be cut until money extension is curbed.
Latest figures show private sector credit growing at 18.86 percent in October compared with 17.36 in October last year.
High interest rates have added to the squeeze on consumers' pockets and raised pressures on retailers' bottomline.
"Higher rates take more spending power out of the consumer's pocket because he has to pay more on a bond (mortgage), a car that he has bought on higher purchase," Pettit said.
South African banks' prime lending rate, currently at 20.25 percent, has risen by a net 1.75 percentage points this year.
Economists expect rates to hold a current high levels for at least the first quarter of the new year, a prospect clothing retailers relish little.
Announcing an almost nine percent drop in first half trading profits to 249 million rand, sector heavyweight Edgars Ltd said of next year:
"There is little prospect of lower interest rates in the short term and retail markets are unlikely to regain momentum before the middle of calendar 1997."
Edgars' shares have slumped from a high of 170 rand in February to a low of 99 rand this month.
Another bellwether clothing firm, Foschini Ltd, last month reported attributable income down over 14 percent to 74.6 million rand in the six months to September 28.

It blamed tough trading conditions on high consumer indebtedness created by a proliferation of credit offerings. Its shares have fallen from a 33.50 rand peak in January to a 13.75 rand trough last week.

Shares in both Pepkor Ltd and Specialty Stores Ltd have shed over 40 percent this year, touching lows in December. Pepkor fell to a bottom of 15 rand on Monday and Specialty to 375 cents on December 4.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
